text: When the asteroid hit about 66 million years ago, roughly three quarters of all species died out. The survivors had a few things in common. Most were small, ate many different foods, and could hide or wait out hard times.

Animals in rivers and lakes did better than those on land. Their food chain started with dead leaves and mud, not with fresh plants needing sunlight. Big animals that needed huge amounts of fresh food had the hardest time.

spots: Ground birds that ate seeds probably survived. Seeds can wait in the soil for years until the sun comes back.
Small furry mammals could hide in burrows and eat almost anything: bugs, roots, seeds.
Crocodiles can go months without eating. They lived in rivers, where food came from rotting leaves, not fresh plants.
Slow, tough and able to rest for long periods. Freshwater turtles did surprisingly well.
Many frogs and salamanders made it. Freshwater places suffered less than land.
Many sharks survived in the oceans too. Sharks are older than the dinosaurs!

quiz.prompt: After the asteroid, forests around the world were destroyed. Which kind of bird is thought to have survived best?

options.t: Birds that lived on the ground
Birds that lived high in trees

quiz.reveal: Studies of fossil plants and birds suggest that forests collapsed for a while. Birds that nested and fed on the ground, eating seeds, did better. The ancestors of ducks, chickens and ostriches were among them.

d.try: Plant a few dried seeds, such as mung beans or mustard seeds, in two cups of soil. Water both, but keep one cup in a dark cupboard for a week and the other by a window. Then move the dark cup into the light. Seeds can wait in the dark for the sun, just as some did after the asteroid.
myth: All the dinosaurs died out 66 million years ago.
Birds are living dinosaurs. One small group of feathered dinosaurs survived the asteroid, and their descendants include every pigeon, parrot and peacock alive today.

sec.t:
The impact threw dust, soot and droplets of sulphur high into the sky. For months, perhaps years, much less sunlight reached the ground. Plants struggled, and many animals that ate plants starved. Then the hunters that ate them starved too.

A [[foodchain|food chain]] is only as strong as its first link. When green plants stopped growing, everything that depended on them was in trouble. That is why the giants, which needed tonnes of fresh food, were hit hardest.

Small animals need less food, can shelter in burrows and holes, and breed quickly. Tiny mammals, many no bigger than a rat, could eat insects, worms, seeds and roots. If one food ran out, they switched.

These survivors became the ancestors of every mammal alive today, from mice to [[@elephants-talk|elephants]] to you. What they did next is the story of the [[@mammals-rise|rise of the mammals]].

[[@living-fossils|Crocodiles]], turtles, frogs and salamanders did surprisingly well. In fresh water, food chains often start with fallen leaves, dead plants and mud, which stay around long after plants stop growing. Water also cools down and warms up slowly, protecting animals from sudden changes.

Crocodiles have another advantage: a big one can go months without eating. Their family has outlasted the dinosaurs by 66 million years so far.

Lizards and [[@lost-titanoboa|snakes]] had a harder time. Studies of fossils from North America suggest most kinds there died out. The few that made it were mostly small.

{{story:croc-ancient}}

Most birds of the time died too, including some toothed kinds. But a few small groups survived. One study suggests that forests were wiped out across much of the world, so birds that lived on the ground did best. Seeds lying in soil gave them food, since [[@seeds-fly|seeds]] can wait for years before sprouting.

From those few survivors came every bird alive today. So the dinosaurs didn't all vanish. [[@lost-passenger-pigeon|A pigeon]] on a balcony in Delhi or a turkey on a farm in Ohio is a living dinosaur.

In the oceans, the great [[@ocean-reptiles|sea reptiles]], like mosasaurs, disappeared, and so did the [[@ammonites|ammonites]], coiled shellfish that had lived for hundreds of millions of years. Many tiny floating creatures at the base of the sea's food chain also died out.

Yet many sharks, bony fish and [[@sea-turtles|sea turtles]] survived. Sharks are older than the dinosaurs, and they have now made it through several mass extinctions.

Survival wasn't only about being clever or strong. Where an animal lived, what it ate and how big it was mattered most. Some scientists add a large helping of luck. A small furry creature in a burrow, in the right place, at the right time, became the starting point for a whole new age.

text: The India Meteorological Department, or IMD, is India's national weather service. It watches the skies, the seas and the air over the whole country, every hour of every day. From that, it makes weather forecasts and warns people about danger.

Its job covers a lot more than whether to carry an umbrella. IMD forecasts the [[@monsoon|monsoon]], which millions of farmers depend on. It tracks cyclones, heatwaves, cold waves, fog and [[@thunderstorms|thunderstorms]]. It gives weather information to airports, ships, farmers and disaster teams. It also keeps long records of India's climate, going back well over a century. The United States has a similar service, the National Weather Service.

st.prompt: IMD uses four colours for weather warnings. Which colour means "take action now"?
st.reveal: Green means no warning. Yellow means watch the weather and stay updated. Orange means be prepared. Red means take action, because dangerous weather is expected.

myth: Weather forecasts are mostly wrong anyway.

sec.t:
In the 1860s, a series of disasters struck India. A huge cyclone hit Calcutta in 1864, and drought caused a terrible famine in Odisha in 1866. The British government decided it needed proper [[@weather-records|weather records]].

IMD was founded in 1875, with Henry Blanford as its first chief. Early weather watchers read thermometers and rain gauges by hand and sent the results by telegraph. In 2025 IMD celebrated 150 years. It is now part of the Ministry of Earth Sciences, with its headquarters at Mausam Bhawan in New Delhi.

Every April, IMD gives its first forecast for the coming monsoon, saying whether rain is likely to be below normal, normal or above normal. It updates the forecast in late May or June.

IMD also announces when the monsoon reaches Kerala, usually around 1 June. Farmers, power companies and governments plan around these forecasts. A weak monsoon can mean lower crops and higher food prices, so the whole country pays attention.

IMD runs a regional centre for the World Meteorological Organization that watches cyclones across the north Indian Ocean, including the Bay of Bengal and the Arabian Sea. It names them from a list suggested by 13 countries in the region. Names such as Phailin, Fani and Biparjoy came from this list.

The biggest success story is in [[@odisha|Odisha]]. In 1999 a super cyclone there killed about 10,000 people. When Cyclone Phailin approached in October 2013, IMD predicted its path and strength days in advance. Officials moved nearly 10 lakh people into shelters. Phailin was just as strong, but the number of deaths was kept to a few dozen.

IMD uses colour codes so warnings are easy to understand. Green means no warning. Yellow means watch the weather. Orange means be prepared. Red means take action. Schools may close, fishing boats stay on shore and disaster teams get ready.

Heat has become a growing concern. IMD now issues [[@heatwaves|heatwave]] warnings that help cities open cooling shelters and change working hours for outdoor workers.

IMD's forecasts now reach people through apps like Mausam and Meghdoot, the second made for farmers. Farmers can get advice about when to sow, spray or harvest. Fishermen receive warnings of high waves.

Some weather is still hard to forecast, especially sudden storms like [[@hailstorms-india|hailstorms]] that grow in less than an hour. For those, IMD issues "nowcasts" covering the next three hours. It's a race against the clouds.

text: A sinkhole is a hole that forms when the ground over an empty space underground collapses. Most sinkholes happen where the rock below is limestone, chalk, gypsum or salt. These [[@rocks-types|rocks]] slowly dissolve in water, while hard rocks such as granite hardly dissolve at all.

Rainwater soaks down through the soil and picks up a little carbon dioxide, which makes it very weakly acidic. Over thousands of years, this water eats away the rock, widening cracks into hollows and caves. The soil above stays put for a while, like a thin crust over an empty pie. When it can no longer hold its own weight, it falls in.

st.prompt: Under which kind of rock do sinkholes most often form?
st.reveal: Limestone. Rainwater picks up a little carbon dioxide and becomes very weakly acidic. Over thousands of years, it dissolves limestone, leaving hidden hollows. Granite and basalt barely dissolve at all.

d.try: Build a small wall of sugar cubes in a tray and cover it with a layer of dry sand. Using a spoon, drip water slowly onto one spot. Watch the sand sag and then suddenly drop as the sugar dissolves underneath. Real sinkholes work the same way, only much more slowly.
myth: Sinkholes appear out of nowhere, in an instant.

The collapse can be sudden, but the hollow underneath usually grows for years or even centuries before the surface gives way. Cracks in walls, tilting fences or small dips in the ground can be early warnings.

sec.t:
Landscapes full of dissolving rock are called [[@earth-stone-forests|karst]]. They are riddled with caves, underground streams and sinkholes, a bit like a slice of [[@food-why-cheese-holes|Swiss cheese]]. Rivers may vanish into the ground and pop out again kilometres away. Karst is where the [[@water-cycle|water cycle]] goes underground in a big way: in some karst regions, people get almost all their drinking water from springs and wells fed by these hidden channels.

India has karst too. At the Belum Caves in Andhra Pradesh, visitors enter through holes in the ground that open into long limestone passages. In the hills of [[@meghalaya|Meghalaya]], rain has carved hundreds of caves, some of the longest in India.

Some sinkholes form gently. As rock dissolves slowly, the ground sags into a bowl shape over many years, and sometimes the bowl fills with water to become a pond. Florida has thousands of round lakes made this way.

Others collapse all at once. In 1981, in Winter Park, Florida, a sinkhole opened up and kept growing for days. It swallowed a house, part of a swimming pool and several cars, and grew to about 100 m wide. The city later turned it into a lake.

In February 2014, a sinkhole opened under the National Corvette Museum in Bowling Green, Kentucky. Eight rare sports cars fell in. Kentucky sits on limestone full of caves, including Mammoth Cave, the longest known cave system in the world. Some of the damaged cars were restored, and the museum now tells the story to visitors.

{{story:roads-built}}

Not every sinkhole is natural. Pumping too much [[@earth-sinking-cities|groundwater]] can drain the water that was helping to hold up the rock and soil. Old mines can collapse. A leaking water pipe or drain can wash soil away under a road until it suddenly caves in, swallowing a car or a bus stop.

In 2010, a deep, round hole about 20 m across opened in the middle of a street in Guatemala City after heavy rain from a tropical storm. Engineers blamed leaking pipes and loose volcanic soil, not limestone. Cities now use radar that sees through the ground to spot hollows under busy [[@roads-built|roads]].

In southern China, enormous sinkholes called tiankeng, meaning "heavenly pits", drop hundreds of metres. Xiaozhai Tiankeng is over 600 m deep. Some have whole forests growing at the bottom, with plants and insects that live nowhere else.

Underwater sinkholes are called blue holes. Dean's Blue Hole in the Bahamas plunges about 200 m. Free divers, who swim down on a single breath, train there because the water is calm and very deep.

text: People could probably visit Mars one day, and maybe stay for a while in sealed bases. Living there for a lifetime, as a real colony, would be extremely hard.

Mars is cold, with an average temperature of about −60 °C. Its air is mostly carbon dioxide, so nobody could breathe it, and so thin that liquid water left in the open would quickly boil away. There is no global magnetic field, so harmful radiation reaches the ground. Dust storms can cover the whole planet. Gravity is only about 38% of Earth's, and nobody knows what living in it for years would do to the human body.
On the other hand, Mars has a day almost the same length as ours, frozen water in the ground and a surface you can stand on. That makes it the most likely place in the solar system for people to try.

st.prompt: Why would Mars settlers probably build their homes underground or under thick layers of soil?

options.t: To shield themselves from harmful radiation

st.reveal: Mars has no global magnetic field and a very thin atmosphere, so radiation from the Sun and deep space reaches the surface. A few metres of soil, rock or ice overhead would block much of it.

n.certNote: Engineers agree that a short human visit to Mars is possible with enough money and effort. Whether people could ever live there long term, and how soon, is hotly debated.

d.try: Plan a Mars base on paper. List everything four people would need for a year, including air, water, food, warmth, power, medicine and something to do. Then cross out anything you think could be made or grown on Mars instead of carried from Earth.
myth: We could give Mars a thick atmosphere and make it like Earth in a few years.

A 2018 NASA-funded study found Mars doesn't have enough carbon dioxide left that can be released to warm it up with today's technology. Turning Mars into a second Earth would take far longer than a human lifetime, if it is possible at all.

sec.t:
Carrying everything from Earth would be hugely expensive, so settlers would need to make things on Mars. NASA's Perseverance rover carried an experiment called MOXIE, about the size of a toaster. Between 2021 and 2023, it pulled carbon dioxide from the Martian air and split off oxygen, proving the idea works on a small scale.

Water could come from ice buried in the soil, especially at middle and high latitudes. Food is harder. Martian soil contains salts called perchlorates that are harmful to people, so it would need cleaning before crops could grow. Plants would also need greenhouses for warmth, air pressure and protection, but they would use [[@photosynthesis|photosynthesis]] just as they do on Earth.

Space agencies test life on Mars without leaving home. In 2023, NASA sealed four volunteers inside a 3D-printed "Mars habitat" in Houston for a year to study how they coped. Other teams have lived in domes on the slopes of a Hawaiian volcano or in remote research stations. Scientists who spend winters in [[@antarctica|Antarctica]] face months of isolation and darkness that are a useful model too.

India has its own Mars connection. In 2014, ISRO's Mars Orbiter Mission, nicknamed Mangalyaan, reached Mars orbit on its first attempt, making India the first Asian country to get a spacecraft there. Its budget was famously small for a planetary mission.

Some people, including the founder of the company [[@reusable-rockets|SpaceX]], say humans should become a "multi-planet species" and want to send large ships to Mars soon. Supporters say a base on Mars would teach us a great deal and protect humanity from disasters on Earth.

Many scientists are more cautious. They point out that even the harshest desert on Earth is far kinder than Mars, and that the money might do more good solving problems here. Others worry about bringing Earth microbes to Mars before we know whether it has life of its own. The first human footprint on Mars may still be decades away, and nobody can say yet whether a child will ever be born there.

text: Most scientists think the Moon was born in a giant crash. About 4.5 billion years ago, when Earth was young, a planet about the size of Mars slammed into it. Scientists have nicknamed this lost planet Theia.

The crash melted huge amounts of rock and flung it into space. That debris formed a ring around Earth. Over time, most of it clumped together into one big ball: the Moon. The biggest clue is in Moon rocks, which match Earth's rocks in some surprising ways.

sec.t:
People have wondered about the Moon's origin for a long time. In the late 1800s, George Darwin, son of the naturalist Charles Darwin, suggested that young Earth spun so fast that a blob flew off and became the Moon. Others thought Earth's [[gravity|gravity]] captured a passing Moon, or that the two formed side by side.

Each idea had problems. A spinning Earth could not have thrown off such a large Moon. A passing body would probably have zoomed past, not been caught. The answer needed better evidence.

Between 1969 and 1972, the [[@apollo-moon|Apollo astronauts]] brought about 382 kg of Moon rock and soil back to Earth. Neil Armstrong and Buzz Aldrin collected the very first samples in July 1969. Scientists studied every crumb closely, and found three big clues.

First, the Moon's rocks have the same chemical fingerprints as Earth's, especially in the kinds of oxygen [[atom|atoms]] they contain. Second, the Moon has very little water and very little iron, with only a small iron [[core|core]]. Third, its [[@rocks-oldest|oldest rocks]] show that its surface was once covered in a deep ocean of molten rock.

In the 1970s, scientists put these clues together. A giant crash could explain them all. It would throw out mostly the rocky outer layers of Earth and Theia, not their iron centres, and the heat would melt everything.

{{story:earth-age}}

The crash idea has one big problem. Computer models suggest that most of the Moon should be made of Theia, not Earth. Yet Moon rocks match Earth's closely. Maybe Theia happened to be made of very similar stuff. Maybe the crash was so violent that the two planets' rock mixed completely in a giant spinning cloud. Scientists are still testing these ideas, which is why the details remain uncertain.

The Moon is slowly moving away from us, about 3.8 cm every year. We know this very precisely because Apollo astronauts [[@moon-landing-sites|left mirrors on the Moon]]. Scientists fire [[@lasers|lasers]] at them and time how long the light takes to bounce back.

Long ago, the Moon was much closer and would have looked much bigger in the sky. Earth also spun faster. Fossil corals about 400 million years old have daily growth lines that suggest a year then had about 400 days, each roughly 22 hours long.

The Moon steadies the tilt of Earth's spin, which helps keep our [[@seasons-why|seasons]] fairly regular over long periods. Its pull [[@moon-tides-life|raises the tides]]. Many animals use moonlight as a clock. On the [[@great-barrier-reef|Great Barrier Reef]], for example, corals release their eggs all together on nights a few days after a full moon. Missions like India's [[@chandrayaan|Chandrayaan-3]] are still studying its rocks, and every new sample adds a clue to the story of its birth.

text: Animals talk without words, using every sense they have. Birds sing and call, wolves howl, and frogs croak to attract mates. [[@ants-world|Ants lay trails of scent]]. [[@power-cuttlefish|Cuttlefish]] flash colour patterns across their skin. Elephants rumble so low that the sound can travel through the ground. Bees dance.

Each message has a job: "danger", "food over here", "this is my patch", "come closer" or "stay away". Some signals are simple. Others carry surprisingly detailed information. Whether any animal has a true language like ours is still argued about, but animals clearly share more than scientists once thought.

st.prompt: A honeybee returns to the hive and does a waggle dance pointing straight up the honeycomb. What is it telling the others?

options.t: Fly towards the Sun to find food

st.reveal: Inside the dark hive, "straight up" stands for the direction of the Sun. A dance angled to the right of straight up means fly to the right of the Sun by the same angle. The longer the waggle part lasts, the farther away the flowers are.

sec.t:
From the 1920s to the 1940s, the Austrian scientist Karl von Frisch spent years watching honeybees in glass-sided hives. He noticed that a bee returning from good flowers would run in a figure-of-eight on the honeycomb, wiggling its body along the middle line.

He worked out that the angle of the wiggle showed the direction to fly compared with the Sun, and its length showed the distance. Other bees followed the dancer, picked up the scent of the flowers and set off. Many scientists at first doubted that an insect could pass on a map. Later experiments confirmed it, and in 1973 von Frisch shared the Nobel Prize. Young bees even seem to get better at [[@bees-dance|the dance]] with practice, by following older dancers.

Some messages travel far. [[@whale-songs|Humpback whales]] sing long songs that can be heard many kilometres away, and all the males in one area sing nearly the same song, which slowly changes each year. Elephants make deep rumbles, some below what human ears can hear, that other elephants can pick up from a few kilometres away.

Other messages stay close. Ants mark a path to food with chemicals called pheromones, and each ant that walks it adds more. Cats rub their cheeks on furniture to leave their scent. Fireflies flash in patterns that tell other fireflies which kind they are.

Human language lets us combine words in endless new ways, and talk about the past, the future and things far away. Bees come close when they describe a place out of sight. Some parrots and apes have learned to use words or symbols taught by people, and [[@parrots-talk|parrots]] can copy speech very well.

Most scientists say no animal has yet shown everything human language does. Others think we have simply not understood animal signals well enough. People who use [[@sign-language|sign language]] show that language doesn't need sound at all, which is one reason researchers keep watching gestures, faces and bodies in animals too.

text: A car begins as giant rolls of [[@steel|steel]], some weighing as much as several elephants. Machines press the steel into doors, roofs and floors. [[@robots|Robots]] weld these panels into a shell, which is painted, and then workers fit the engine, wheels, seats, wires and glass. At the end, every car is driven, tested and sprayed with water to check for leaks.
The whole job happens on an assembly line, where the car moves past stations and each team does one task. A large plant can finish a new car roughly every minute, all day.

Robots do most of the welding and painting, which are heavy, hot or messy jobs. People still do much of the final assembly, fitting wires, seats and dashboards, because those tasks need careful hands.

sec.t:
The first stop is the press shop. Steel unrolls from coils, is cut into flat sheets and fed into presses as tall as a two-storey house. A press slams down with a force of hundreds or even thousands of tonnes and stamps a sheet into the curved shape of a bonnet or door in a second or two.

It is loud. Workers wear ear protection, and the floor shakes with each stroke.

In the body shop, the pressed panels meet. Hundreds of robot arms grip, turn and weld them, with sparks flying in showers. A single car body is held together by several thousand spot welds, small points where metal is melted together by an electric current.

The result is a bare metal shell with no paint, engine or seats. Car makers call it the "body in white", probably because early car bodies were primed in a pale colour.

Final assembly is where people take over. The painted body moves slowly along the line while workers fit wiring harnesses, the bundles of wire that work like a car's nervous system. Then come the dashboard, seats, glass, lights and wheels.

The big moment is called "the marriage". The body is lowered on to the engine and axles from below, and bolted together. For an [[@electric-cars|electric car]], the marriage joins the body to a flat battery pack under the floor.

Parts arrive from hundreds of suppliers, sometimes only hours before they are needed. If one lorry of seats is late, the whole line can stop.

sec.h: The line that changed the world
sec.t:
In 1913, Henry Ford's factory near Detroit in the USA set up a moving assembly line for the Model T. Instead of workers walking around a car, the car came to them on a chain. Building a chassis dropped from about 12 hours to about an hour and a half. Cars became cheap enough for ordinary families, and Ford made about 15 million Model Ts.

Before that, the first cars were mostly built by hand, one at a time, as you can see in the story of [[@cars-history|early cars]].

India sold a record of about 45 lakh passenger vehicles in 2025, making it one of the biggest car markets on Earth. Factories in Gurugram, Pune, Chennai and Sanand build cars for India and for ships to Africa, the Middle East and beyond. Chennai is sometimes called the Detroit of India.

Every new design is also crashed on purpose. Test cars smash into barriers carrying dummies packed with sensors, which record forces no person could safely feel. Yet the hardest-working part of most cars stays hidden under the bonnet, where a petrol [[@cars-engine|engine]] sets off thousands of tiny explosions every minute.

text: A pulley is a [[@wheel-invented|wheel]] with a groove around its edge for a rope. By itself, a single pulley fixed to a beam doesn't make a load lighter. What it does is let you pull *down* to lift something *up*. That's easier, because you can use your own body weight to help. This is how a flag goes up a flagpole and how a bucket comes up a village well.

The real magic happens when a pulley moves with the load. Now the load hangs from two lengths of rope instead of one, and each holds half the weight. Add more pulleys and more rope, and the load is shared between even more strands. With four strands, you pull with only a quarter of the force. The catch is that you must pull four times as much rope.

st.prompt: A bucket of sand weighs 20 kg. You lift it with one movable pulley. About how hard do you have to pull?
st.reveal: A movable pulley shares the load between two lengths of rope, so each holds about half. You pull with the force of about 10 kg, but to raise the bucket by 1 metre you must pull 2 metres of rope. Friction makes it a little harder in real life.

sec.t:
The Greek thinker Archimedes, who lived in Syracuse in Sicily over 2,200 years ago, studied levers and pulleys. The writer Plutarch tells a story about him written down about three centuries later. King Hiero challenged Archimedes to show what his machines could do. Archimedes rigged up a system of pulleys and, sitting calmly, drew a fully loaded ship onto the shore with one hand.

We can't be sure the story happened exactly that way. But the physics is sound. With enough pulleys, one person really can move something far heavier than themselves. It just takes a lot of rope and patience.

Look up at a building site and you will see pulleys on top of tall cranes. Steel cables run over them, so the crane's motor can lift tonnes of concrete. [[@elevators|Lifts]] in tall buildings hang from steel ropes running over a big pulley wheel, with a heavy counterweight on the other side to balance the car.

Sailing ships once carried hundreds of pulleys, called blocks, so sailors could raise heavy sails by hand. Gyms use pulleys in weight machines. Window blinds and old-style curtain cords use them too.

Many [[@villages-india|Indian villages]] drew water from deep open wells. A rope ran over a simple pulley, often called a *ghirni* in Hindi, fixed to a frame above the well. The pulley let people pull downward with their body weight instead of hauling each pot straight up, hand over hand.

The builders of India's [[@architecture-temples|great stone temples]] and Egypt's [[@pyramids|pyramids]] probably used ramps, levers and simple lifting frames to raise heavy blocks. Exactly how they did it is not always recorded. Whatever the method, they were using the same rule a pulley follows: a smaller push, spread over a longer distance, can move almost anything.

text: Garba is a circle dance from Gujarat, performed during Navratri, the nine-night Hindu festival honouring the goddess Durga in her many forms. Dancers move around a clay pot with a lamp inside, clapping and turning in rhythm.

The dancing goes late for several reasons. Navratri is a night festival by tradition, with prayers, called aarti, in the evening. The nine nights are a time of devotion, but also of joy, music and meeting friends. Autumn nights are cool after a hot day. And once the drums get going and the circle speeds up, few people want to stop. In big cities, the music often runs past midnight, though local rules now set time limits for loudspeakers.

st.reveal: The pot, called a garbo, has holes all over it and a small oil lamp, or diya, inside. People see the flame as a symbol of life and of the goddess. Dancers move around it in circles, always facing in towards the light.

sec.t:
The word *garba* comes from *garbha*, the Sanskrit word for womb. The clay pot in the middle is called a *garbo*. It has holes punched all over it and a small lamp burning inside, so dots of light shine out in the dark.

Many people see the pot as a symbol of the body, the womb or the universe, and the flame as life and the goddess's power. Dancing in a circle around it is a form of worship. Circles can grow into rings within rings, hundreds of people moving together, always facing in towards the light.

Dancers dress up. Women often wear a *chaniya choli*, a wide, swirling skirt with a short blouse, covered in mirror work and embroidery from Kutch. Men wear a *kediyu*, a short pleated top, with a turban or cap. Many outfits use tie-dyed [[@art-bandhani|bandhani]] cloth.

Each of the nine nights has its own colour in many cities, and people try to match it. Shops and tailors in Gujarat stay busy for weeks before Navratri.

Garba began as a dance by women in village courtyards and temple grounds. Over the last century, it moved into city squares, party plots and stadiums. Vadodara's big garba events draw tens of thousands of dancers on a single night. Rehearsal classes start months early. In Ahmedabad and Surat, garba classes fill school halls and rooftops on summer evenings as people learn the newest steps.

In 2023, UNESCO added "Garba of Gujarat" to its list of Intangible Cultural Heritage, which honours living traditions, not buildings. It was India's 15th entry on that list.

Wherever Gujarati families have settled, garba has followed. New Jersey, Texas, London, Toronto and Nairobi all hold Navratri nights, some in hired sports halls packed with thousands. Many dancers there have never been to Gujarat, but they know every step.

During Navratri, the same nine nights are celebrated very differently across India. Bengal honours Durga with pandals and idols in [[@durga-puja|Durga Puja]], while Gujarat dances. And after nine nights of garba, many Gujarati families celebrate Dussehra, the tenth day, with a plate of crunchy fafda and syrupy jalebi, one of the best-loved pairings in [[@gujarati-food|Gujarati food]].

text: Most people choose jobs by mixing what they enjoy, what they are good at, what they can train for, and what work is available where they live. Money matters, and so do family hopes, the example of people they admire, and plain luck.

Few people pick one job at 15 and keep it forever. Many change direction several times. In a long American study, people born between 1957 and 1964 held about 12 different jobs, on average, by their mid-50s. Careers often look like a winding path rather than a straight road.

sec.t:
Career counsellors often start with three questions. What do you like doing? What are you good at, or willing to get good at? And what matters to you: helping people, making things, earning well, being outdoors, or having a steady routine?

An American psychologist, John Holland, sorted interests into six broad types, such as people who like working with tools, with ideas, with people or with data. Many career tests still use his ideas. They are not fortune-tellers, but they can point to jobs worth exploring.

In India, many people follow their family's trade, such as farming, running a shop or [[@knitting-weaving|weaving]]. More than half of India's workers are self-employed, running their own small farms or businesses instead of working for a company. In the past, caste often decided what work a person could do. [[@constitution|The Constitution]] banned that discrimination, though its effects have not fully disappeared.

Where you live matters too. A coastal town offers [[@fishing-boats|fishing]] and shipping work. A big city has offices, hospitals and film studios. And chance plays a part: [[@jobs-teacher|a good teacher]], a summer job or a book can change someone's direction completely.

Some jobs keep their names but change completely. A farmer today may use a phone app to check the weather and crop prices, and a doctor may study scans made by machines that did not exist 50 years ago. Even teachers now use smartboards and online lessons.

New technologies create jobs that nobody imagined before. [[@jobs-pilot|Pilots]] appeared after the [[@wright-brothers|Wright brothers]] flew. App designers, video editors and [[@drones-delivery|drone operators]] are recent. The [[@industrial-revolution|Industrial Revolution]] wiped out some hand crafts but created millions of factory jobs. Today, people are debating what [[@robots|robots]] and [[@ai-what|artificial intelligence]] will do. Some jobs will shrink, some will change, and new ones will appear. Experts disagree on how fast.

Nobody can predict exactly which jobs will exist. So many advisers suggest building skills that travel well: reading carefully, writing clearly, working with numbers, getting along with others and learning new things quickly. Trying things out helps too. A school project, a hobby or [[@volunteering|volunteering]] can show you what you enjoy long before you have to choose. Grace Hopper, a pioneer of computer programming, started as a maths teacher.

text: People greet each other in hundreds of ways. Some touch, some don't. Indians often say namaste with palms pressed together. Americans shake hands or wave. Japanese people bow. French friends kiss on the cheek. Maori in New Zealand press noses and foreheads. In parts of Tibet, people traditionally stick out their tongues.

Each greeting says the same basic things: I see you, I'm friendly, I mean no harm. The way it's done depends on history, religion, climate, closeness and who is older. Even within India, one family may say *vanakkam*, another *sat sri akal*, another *salaam* or *khamma ghani*.

sec.t:
*Namaste* comes from Sanskrit and is often explained as "I bow to you". Palms are pressed together near the chest, sometimes with a small bow. It is common across India and Nepal, and during the COVID-19 pandemic people around the world started using it because it needs no touching.

In Thailand, the *wai* looks similar, but the height of the hands matters. The higher they go, the more respect is shown. Monks and elders get the highest wai.

The handshake is common in Europe, America and offices everywhere. A popular theory says it began as a way to show that your hand held no weapon, but historians aren't sure. More of that puzzle lives in the story of [[@life-handshake|the handshake]].

In Japan, bowing is a whole language. A small nod for a friend. A deeper bow of around 30 degrees for a teacher. An even deeper, slower bow to say a serious sorry. [[@japan-culture|Japanese culture]] has many rules like this, learned from childhood.

In France, friends greet with *la bise*, touching cheeks and making a kissing sound. How many kisses? It depends on the region: one, two, three or even four.

The Maori *hongi* is a press of noses and foreheads. Tradition says it shares the *ha*, the breath of life. Visitors to official events in [[@new-zealand|New Zealand]], including prime ministers and royals, often receive a hongi.

{{story:life-handshake}}

In Tibet, showing the tongue has long been a sign of respect. A story often told says a cruel 9th-century king, Langdarma, had a black tongue. People showed their tongues to prove they weren't him reborn. It's a legend, but the custom is real, mostly among older people in villages.

Muslims around the world often greet each other with *As-salaam alaikum*, "peace be upon you". It is answered with *Wa alaikum as-salaam*, "and upon you be peace". Hands may be placed on the heart.

Greetings can cause confusion. A firm handshake that feels confident in the USA can seem pushy elsewhere. In some places, men and women don't touch when they greet unless they are family. Looking someone in the eye is friendly in some cultures and rude in others when facing an elder.

Travellers learn to watch first and copy. Business guides teach people how to greet before they visit another country. Getting a greeting right is a small sign of [[@cultures-respect|respect for other cultures]].

Deaf people greet each other in [[@sign-language|sign language]], which has its own word for hello, different in every sign language. Indian Sign Language and American Sign Language are not the same. In many places, a simple wave, a smile or raised eyebrows does the job without any words at all.

text: Cryptography is the science of scrambling a message so only the right person can read it. The scrambling method is called a [[cipher|cipher]], and the secret setting that opens it is called the key.

For most of history, ciphers were clever word games. Today they are built from maths, especially [[@prime-numbers|prime numbers]]. Your phone uses this maths every time you send a message, log in to a website or make a payment, so that anyone listening in sees only nonsense.

st.prompt: In English writing, which letter turns up most often? Code-breakers use this to crack simple ciphers.
st.reveal: E is the most common letter in ordinary English text. If a secret message swaps every letter for another, the symbol that appears most often probably stands for E, and the rest of the cipher starts to fall apart.

sec.h: Caesar's shift and how it broke
sec.t:
The Roman writer Suetonius tells us that Julius Caesar wrote secret letters by shifting each letter three places along the alphabet. A became D, B became E, and so on. It fooled people who weren't expecting it.

But shift ciphers, and even ciphers that swap every letter for a random symbol, have a weakness. In any language, some letters appear far more than others. Around the 800s CE, the Arab scholar al-Kindi described how to count the symbols in a secret message and match the most common ones to the most common letters. This method, called frequency analysis, cracked simple ciphers for centuries.

Old ciphers had one big problem. Both people needed the same secret key, so they had to meet or send it somehow without anyone stealing it.

In 1976 and 1977, researchers in the USA published a way around this, called public-key cryptography. Think of a padlock. You hand out open padlocks to anyone who asks. They snap your padlock shut on a box, but only you have the key to open it. Anyone can lock the box, but only one person can open it.

The best-known version, RSA, is named after Ron Rivest, Adi Shamir and Leonard Adleman. Its padlock is a giant number made by multiplying two secret primes. Multiplying is easy. Splitting the giant number back into its two primes is extremely hard if the primes are hundreds of digits long.

That one-way trick protects online shopping, [[@email|email]] and payments, including India's [[@upi-payments|UPI system]]. The small padlock beside a website's address in your browser means your connection is being scrambled. Strong [[@passwords|passwords]] add another lock on top.

Mathematicians keep checking whether anyone has found a shortcut. One worry is the [[@quantum-computers|quantum computer]], which in theory could factor huge numbers fast. Cryptographers are already designing new ciphers based on different maths problems, so they are ready before such machines get powerful enough.

sec.h: Hide the key, not the method
sec.t: In 1883, a Dutch-born teacher named Auguste Kerckhoffs wrote down a rule that cryptographers still follow. A good cipher should stay safe even if the enemy knows exactly how it works. Only the key needs to be secret. That is why the maths behind RSA is printed in textbooks, and anyone can check it for weaknesses.

text: Climbers scale cliffs by finding small holds for their hands and feet: cracks, ledges, bumps and pockets in the rock. They push up with their legs, balance their weight over their feet and use their arms mostly to stay close to the wall. Sticky rubber shoes and chalked hands give them grip.

For safety, most climbers use a rope tied to a harness. As they climb, they clip the rope into metal bolts or devices jammed into cracks. A partner on the ground, called a belayer, holds the rope with a braking device. If the climber slips, they fall only a short way before the rope catches them.

st.reveal: The climber clips the rope into metal bolts on the wall as they go up. A partner called a belayer holds the other end with a braking device, so a fall stops at the last bolt clipped.

sec.t:
Climbing shoes are tight, flat and made of special rubber that grips like a pencil eraser on paper. A good climber can stand on a ledge narrower than a coin. That is [[@friction|friction]] doing the work. The more weight pressed onto the rubber, the better it holds.

Hands sweat, and sweat makes rock slippery. So climbers carry a bag of chalk on their belt. The white powder is magnesium carbonate, which soaks up moisture. Look at a popular cliff and you can spot the routes by the white smudges left on the holds.

sec.h: Three ways to climb a wall

sec.t:
In California's [[@yosemite|Yosemite]] valley stands El Capitan, a smooth granite wall about 900 metres high. That is taller than the Burj Khalifa, the world's tallest building. Most teams take three to five days to climb it. They sleep in hanging tents called portaledges, bolted to the cliff, with hundreds of metres of air below.

In 2017, Alex Honnold climbed El Capitan with no rope at all, in under four hours. This is called free soloing, and almost no one tries it, because a single mistake would be deadly. Most climbers, even world champions, prefer a rope.

India has some superb rock. [[@hampi|Hampi]] in Karnataka is famous for its giant granite boulders, piled up around ancient temple ruins. Climbers from around the world come to try its short, tricky problems in the winter months. Badami's red sandstone cliffs and the rocky hills near Bengaluru also draw climbers.

Indoor climbing gyms have opened in cities like Mumbai, Delhi, Pune and Bengaluru. Many schools now have small walls too. Indian climbers compete at Asian and world events, and the sport is growing fast.

The best climbers on Earth aren't human. Mountain goats balance on cliff ledges as narrow as a hand. Geckos run up glass and across ceilings with no claws or glue, using millions of tiny hairs on their toes. Engineers are copying [[@power-gecko-feet|gecko feet]] to make sticky pads for robots that might one day climb buildings without any rope at all.

text: Indian wrestlers have won eight [[@olympics-india|Olympic]] medals. The story began in 1952, when K. D. Jadhav won bronze in Helsinki, independent India's first individual Olympic medal. The next medal took 56 years, but since Sushil Kumar's bronze in 2008, Indian wrestlers have won medals at every Summer Olympics up to 2024.

The medals grew out of India's long tradition of kushti, wrestling in mud pits called akharas. They also came from the hard work of coaches, families and village communities, especially in Haryana and Maharashtra.

Olympic wrestlers compete in weight classes, so they face opponents of similar size. Balance, speed, technique and stamina often matter more than raw strength.

sec.t:
Kushti, also called pehlwani, is centuries old. Wrestlers, called pehlwans, train in an akhara, a pit of soft earth under a guru. They wake before dawn, do hundreds of squats and push-ups, swing heavy wooden clubs and wrestle for hours.

Their diet is famous: milk, [[@butter-ghee|ghee]], almonds and plenty of roti. In the early 1900s a pehlwan known as the Great Gama became world famous. He was never defeated in a long career, and in 1910 he went to London and won a big international contest.

From the 1980s, Delhi's Chhatrasal Stadium, under the coach Satpal Singh, trained many top wrestlers. One was Sushil Kumar, who won bronze in Beijing in 2008 and silver in London in 2012. He was the first Indian since independence to win two individual Olympic medals.

In London, Yogeshwar Dutt also won bronze. At Rio in 2016, Sakshi Malik became the first Indian woman to win an Olympic wrestling medal. At Tokyo, Ravi Kumar Dahiya won silver and Bajrang Punia bronze. In Paris in 2024, 21-year-old Aman Sehrawat won bronze.

Women's wrestling met resistance in many Haryana villages, where girls were expected to stay at home. Mahavir Singh Phogat trained his daughters anyway. Geeta Phogat won gold at the 2010 [[@commonwealth-games|Commonwealth Games]], the first Indian woman wrestler to do so. The [[@bollywood|Bollywood]] film *Dangal* (2016) told their story and was a hit in India and China.

His niece Vinesh Phogat became one of India's best wrestlers. At Paris 2024 she reached the final, but was disqualified on the morning of the final for being 100 grams over the weight limit. It was a heartbreaking moment for Indian fans.

Olympic wrestling has weight classes, so wrestlers must "make weight" by stepping on the scales. Many cut weight before a competition by sweating and eating less, which can be hard on the body. Experts warn young athletes to do this only with proper supervision.

The sport has moved from mud to mats, and from local dangals, village wrestling contests, to world championships. Yet many Olympic wrestlers still start in an akhara, where the earth is soft and the day begins before sunrise.

text: Your skin is a waterproof, stretchy coat that keeps your insides in and the outside world out. It blocks most germs, stops you drying out, and protects you from some of the Sun's harmful rays.
It also works as a thermostat and a sense organ. It sweats to cool you down, and it's packed with nerve endings that feel touch, heat, cold and pain.
Spread flat, an adult's skin would cover about 1.5 to 2 square metres, roughly the size of a single bed. That makes it the largest organ in your body.

d.try: Press a piece of clear sticky tape onto the back of your hand, peel it off and stick it onto dark paper. Look at it with a magnifying glass. The faint flakes you see are dead skin cells from the very top layer of your skin.
myth: People with dark skin can't get sunburnt.
Darker skin has more melanin, which blocks more sunlight, so it burns less easily. But anyone can get sunburnt with enough strong sun. Shade, a hat and sunscreen help everyone.
facts: on the soles of your feet

sec.t:
The top layer, the *epidermis*, is thinner than a sheet of paper in most places. Its outer surface is made of flat, dead cells packed with a tough protein. They form a protective shield and [[@gross-skin-shedding|flake away constantly]]. Fresh cells are made at the bottom of the epidermis and work their way up, so the outer layer is replaced roughly every month.

Below is the *dermis*. It holds blood vessels, nerve endings, [[@hair-grow|hair]] roots and sweat glands. Its stretchy fibres let skin spring back when you pinch it. As people grow very old, these fibres weaken, which is one reason skin gets wrinkles.

At the bottom is a layer of fat that keeps you warm and cushions you when you fall.

Skin is thickest on the soles of your feet and the palms of your hands, which take the most rubbing. It's thinnest on your eyelids. People who often walk barefoot grow even thicker soles for protection, a bit like a natural pair of chappals.

Your palms and soles also have ridges, which [[@body-pruney-fingers|give you grip]]. On your fingertips they form your [[@fingerprints|fingerprints]], and no two people's are the same, not even identical [[@twins|twins]]'.

Skin colour comes mostly from [[melanin|melanin]], a dark pigment made by special cells. Everyone has about the same number of these cells. People with darker skin have cells that make more melanin, or a darker kind of it.

Melanin works as a natural sunshade against ultraviolet light from the [[@sun-what|Sun]]. Scientists such as the American anthropologist Nina Jablonski think darker skin evolved where sunlight is strongest, near the equator, and lighter skin where it's weaker. Lighter skin may help people make enough vitamin D in places with little sun, because skin uses sunlight to make it. Tanning is your skin making more melanin after time in the sun.

An [[@octopus-smart|octopus]] goes much further. Its skin has [[@ocean-mimic-octopus|colour sacs]] it can open and close in a fraction of a second.

When you cut yourself, your skin starts repairing right away. Blood clots seal the cut, and a [[@scabs|scab]] forms on top like a temporary bandage. Underneath, new cells crawl in from the edges to close the gap. Small cuts often heal in about a week. Keeping a cut clean helps it heal well, and a doctor or trusted adult can check one that looks red, swollen or sore.

text: Sunlight carries invisible rays called ultraviolet, or UV. Too much UV damages the DNA inside skin cells. Your body reacts by sending extra blood to the area, which makes it red, hot and sore. Damaged cells die, and a few days later the skin peels. That is a sunburn.

Sunscreen puts a thin layer between your [[@skin|skin]] and those rays. Some sunscreens contain minerals, such as zinc oxide, that block UV at the surface. Others contain chemicals that soak up UV and turn its energy into a tiny amount of harmless heat. Either way, less UV gets through to the living cells underneath.

st.prompt: On a cloudy day, how much of the sun's UV can still reach your skin?
st.reveal: Thin or broken cloud blocks a lot of light and heat, so it feels gentle, but up to about 80 per cent of UV can pass through. That is why people often get badly burned on grey days at the beach.

myth: People with dark skin can't get sunburned and don't need sun protection.
More melanin gives darker skin extra protection, so it burns less easily, but it can still burn in strong sun. Doctors advise everyone to protect their skin and eyes when the UV index is high.
facts: about every 2 hours, and after swimming

sec.h: What the numbers on the bottle mean
sec.t:
SPF stands for "sun protection factor". It measures protection against UVB. An SPF 15 sunscreen blocks about 93 per cent of UVB, SPF 30 about 97 per cent and SPF 50 about 98 per cent. No sunscreen blocks all of it.

The words "broad spectrum" mean it also guards against UVA. Those tests assume a thick layer. Most people use far less than the testers do, and sunscreen rubs off with sweat, towels and water. That is why doctors say to apply it generously and again every two hours, and after swimming.

A common guide for an adult's whole body is about a shot glass full, roughly 30 millilitres, or about a teaspoon for the face and neck. Children need less, but the idea is the same. A thin smear does far less than the label promises.

Skin has its own defence: a dark pigment called [[melanin|melanin]]. It sits inside skin cells like a little umbrella over the DNA. People with darker [[@skin-colour|skin colour]] have more melanin, which is why they burn less easily.

A tan is skin making extra melanin after UV has already done some damage. It is a sign of injury, not of health. A tan gives only a little extra protection, about the same as a very weak sunscreen. Summer sun also brings out [[@freckles-moles|freckles]], which are small patches of extra melanin.

sec.h: Shade, hats and the UV index
sec.t:
Sunscreen works best as one tool among several. Shade, a wide hat, sunglasses and loose clothes with long sleeves all block UV well, and they don't wash off in the pool. Many weather apps now show the UV index, a scale created with help from the World Health Organization. At 3 or above, protection is a good idea. In Indian summers it often climbs past 10.

Sand and water reflect some UV back up at you, and fresh snow reflects most of it. The sun isn't all bad, though. Your skin uses a little UVB to make [[@vitamins|vitamin D]], which keeps bones strong. A short time outdoors is enough for most children, without getting burned.

The modern SPF scale was popularised in the 1970s by an Austrian chemist, Franz Greiter. According to his company's story, he had been badly burned while climbing a mountain in the Alps called Piz Buin, and he named his sunscreen after it.

text: Daily life in ancient Greece depended on who you were and which city you lived in. In Athens, around 2,500 years ago, a citizen man might farm, trade or make things, then spend time in the agora, the open marketplace, talking politics and shopping. Citizen women mostly ran the household and rarely went out alone.

Many of the hardest jobs were done by enslaved people, captured in war or bought. Food was simple: barley bread or porridge, olives, figs, cheese, fish and wine mixed with water. Meat was usually eaten at religious festivals, after an animal had been offered to the gods.

st.prompt: What did the winner of an event at the ancient Olympic Games receive at Olympia itself?
st.reveal: Winners at Olympia were crowned with a wreath cut from a sacred olive tree. Back home, though, their cities often gave them free meals, statues and other rewards for life.

n.certNote: Most of what we know comes from Athens, and from books written by wealthy men. Life for women, enslaved people, farmers and people in other city-states is much harder to see, and numbers such as how many people were enslaved are estimates.

myth: Ancient Greek statues and temples were always plain white marble.
Traces of paint show that many statues and buildings were brightly coloured. Over the centuries the paint wore away, leaving the bare stone we see in museums.

sec.t:
Boys from families who could pay started school at about seven. An enslaved servant called a *paidagogos* walked them there and kept an eye on them. From him we get the word "pedagogy", the art of teaching.

Pupils learned to read and write, often scratching letters on wax tablets with a pointed stick. They memorised long passages of Homer's poems, learned to play the lyre and sing, and spent hours at the gymnasium running and wrestling. Girls were usually taught at home, learning to spin, weave and manage a household. In Sparta things were different: girls there exercised outdoors too, which shocked visitors from Athens.

Every four years, Greeks from rival cities travelled to Olympia, a sanctuary of Zeus in the west of Greece. Tradition says the first recorded Games took place in 776 BCE. A sacred truce let athletes and visitors travel safely.

The oldest event was the *stadion*, a sprint of about 190 metres, roughly two lengths of a football field. Later came wrestling, boxing, the pentathlon and [[@wheel-to-chariot|chariot races]]. Athletes competed naked. Married women could not watch, but owners of winning horses counted as champions, so in 396 BCE the Spartan princess Kyniska became an Olympic victor through her chariot team. The Games carried on for over a thousand years, until about 393 CE.

Religion was part of every day. Families kept a small altar at home and poured a little wine as an offering before meals. Cities held festivals with processions, sacrifices, music and plays. In Athens, these festivals gave birth to [[@theatre|theatre]], with actors in masks performing tragedies and comedies in vast open-air theatres.

People asked the gods for help with harvests, journeys, illnesses and love. Stories of Zeus, Athena and the other [[@greek-myths|Greek gods]] were told at home long before children ever read them.

Most of what we know comes from writers in Athens, nearly all wealthy men. Enslaved people, poor farmers and most women left few words of their own. Historians estimate that enslaved people may have made up a large share of Athens's population, but the true number is unknown. Archaeology helps fill the gap: a child's toy, a loom weight or a worn cooking pot speaks for people the books left out.

text: They used relays. Instead of one messenger travelling the whole way, kings set up a chain of stations along the main roads. A fresh runner or rider waited at each one. When a message arrived, it was handed on at once, and the next person set off at full speed.

This system, called *dak*, could carry news across the country many times faster than any traveller. It served the court, the army and tax officials, not ordinary families. Ordinary people sent letters with traders, pilgrims or friends heading the right way.

st.prompt: In Ibn Battuta's India, which was faster for news, the horse post or the foot post?

options.t: Both took exactly the same time

st.reveal: Ibn Battuta wrote that the foot post was quicker. Runners worked in short relays, each sprinting only about a third of a mile before handing on, so nobody ever slowed down from tiredness.

d.try: Set up a relay with friends in a park or playground with an adult nearby. First, one person runs the whole distance with a folded note. Then split it into short stretches with a handover at each. Time both. Which is faster, and why?
myth: Before the British came, India had no organised postal system.

Indian rulers ran messenger and relay systems for centuries. The Delhi Sultanate, Sher Shah Suri and the Mughals all used chains of runners and riders, though these served mainly the government, not ordinary people.
facts: Sarais along Sher Shah Suri's roads
Local name for a royal messenger

sec.t:
The best description comes from Ibn Battuta, a traveller from Morocco who reached Delhi in 1334 and worked for Sultan Muhammad bin Tughlaq. He wrote that the sultan had two kinds of post.

The horse post used royal horses changed every few miles. The foot post used runners. There was a station every third of a mile, about the length of four cricket grounds laid end to end. Each runner held a rod with copper bells at one end. When the next runner heard the bells coming, he got ready, grabbed the letter and sprinted off.

According to [[@ibn-battuta|Ibn Battuta]], news from Sindh reached Delhi in about five days, though the same journey took travellers about fifty.

sec.h: Fruit and holy water by post
sec.t:
The relay carried more than letters. Ibn Battuta says it brought the sultan fresh fruit from Khurasan, in what is now Iran and Afghanistan. When the court moved to Daulatabad in the Deccan, runners carried water from the Ganga for the sultan to drink, a trip of around forty days for ordinary travellers.

The system also worked as a spy network. Officials sent reports on everything happening in the provinces, so the [[@delhi-sultanate|Delhi Sultanate]] could act on trouble quickly.

The idea of a relay post is very old. The Persian Empire ran a royal road with horse stations more than 2,500 years ago, and the Greek writer Herodotus admired its riders. Rome had its own state post. In the USA, the Pony Express did the same thing across the Wild West in 1860 and 1861, with riders changing horses about every 15 to 25 km.

{{story:usa-pony-express}}

In the 1540s, Sher Shah Suri ruled north India for only about five years, but he built fast. He improved the great road that ran from Bengal towards the Khyber Pass, later called the Grand Trunk Road. Along it, by tradition, stood about 1,700 *sarais*, or rest houses, each with wells, food and horses waiting for messengers.

Messengers changing horses at these sarais could carry news from Bengal to the north-west far faster than before. The [[@mughals|Mughals]] kept and expanded the system. Their messengers, called *harkaras*, also gathered news and gossip for the emperor.

The Mughals used pigeons too. Akbar is said to have kept thousands of them, and trained birds could carry short messages between forts and cities far faster than any runner. Pigeon post stayed in use in India for centuries, and police in Odisha were still using pigeons to send messages in remote areas until 2008.

When the East India Company took over, it kept using runners, many carrying a spear and a string of bells to warn off wild animals at night. Each runner covered one stage of road, often at night, before passing his bag on.

In 1854, the British set up a single postal department for all of India, with stamps anyone could buy. Runners still carried mail to remote villages well into the 1900s. Today India Post has around 1.6 lakh post offices (2024 count), more than any other country. And by the 1850s, a new kind of messenger had begun to push the runners aside: electric signals racing down the [[@telegraph|telegraph]] wire.

text: Savitribai Phule was a teacher, poet and social reformer from Maharashtra. In 1848, with her husband Jyotirao Phule, she started a school for girls in Pune at a time when most people thought girls did not need to read. She is often called India's first woman teacher in a modern school.
She also opened schools for children from communities that had been shut out of education because of their caste. She cared for widows, wrote poems, and died in 1897 helping people sick with plague.

st.reveal: Many people in Pune were angry that a woman was teaching girls, and some threw mud, stones and dung at her. She changed into a clean sari when she reached school and kept teaching.

d.try: Ask an older woman in your family, or a neighbour, how many years she went to school and what her classroom was like. Write down three things that were different from your school. Compare answers with a friend who asked someone else.
myth: Girls in India always had the same chance as boys to go to school.
In the early 1800s very few Indian girls learned to read, and many people opposed it. Reformers like the Phules had to fight hard, and girls' schooling only spread widely in the twentieth century.
facts: Girls' school at Bhide Wada, Pune
marked in Maharashtra as Balika Din (Girls' Day)

sec.t:
Savitribai was born in 1831 in Naigaon, a village near Satara. Like most girls of her time, she was married very young, at about nine, to Jyotirao, who was about thirteen. She had never been to school.

Jyotirao believed education could change lives, and he taught her at home. Later she trained as a teacher in Ahmednagar and Pune. In the 1840s this was almost unheard of for an Indian woman.

On 1 January 1848 the Phules opened a school for girls in Bhide Wada, a house in [[@pune|Pune]]. Savitribai taught there. Every day, as she walked to school, some people shouted at her and threw mud, stones or dung. They believed she was breaking the rules of society.

She carried a spare sari in her bag and changed when she arrived. Then she taught. Some accounts say a man once blocked her path, and she slapped him. The harassment slowly eased after that. Her friend Fatima Sheikh, who also became a teacher, worked with her. By the early 1850s the Phules were running several schools in Pune, with well over a hundred girls.

Their lessons were practical. Pupils learned reading, arithmetic, grammar, geography and some science, much like a school today. The Phules also worried about children dropping out, a problem India still works on. They tried paying small stipends to keep poor pupils in class, and they held regular meetings with parents to explain why learning mattered.

{{story:school-history}}

Indian society was divided by [[@caste-history|caste]], and people from the lowest-ranked groups were often not allowed to study at all. The Phules opened schools for their children too, and taught them alongside others.

Many in their own community turned against them. At one point the couple had to leave Jyotirao's family home. They kept going. In 1852 the British government in Bombay Presidency publicly honoured them for their work in education.

In the nineteenth century, many young widows were treated harshly and some were driven from their homes. In 1863 the Phules opened a shelter where widows could safely give birth and leave their babies to be cared for. They later adopted a widow's son, Yashwantrao, who grew up to become a doctor.

Savitribai also wrote poetry. Her first book, *Kavya Phule*, came out in 1854. Its poems urged people, especially girls and the poor, to learn to read. After Jyotirao died in 1890, she led the Satyashodhak Samaj, the society he had founded to fight caste unfairness.

In 1897 bubonic plague swept through Pune. Savitribai and her son set up a clinic outside the city. She carried a sick boy there herself, caught the disease and died on 10 March 1897.

Today her birthday, 3 January, is celebrated in Maharashtra as Balika Din, or Girls' Day. In 2014 the University of Pune was renamed Savitribai Phule Pune University. Thinkers like [[@ambedkar|B.R. Ambedkar]] later carried forward the Phules' fight for equal rights, and [[@jyotirao-phule|Jyotirao Phule]] and Savitribai are often remembered together.

text: English uses 26 letters that stand for sounds. Chinese works differently. Each character stands for one syllable, and that syllable usually carries a meaning. The character 山 is pronounced *shān* and means mountain. 火 is *huǒ*, fire.

Some words are a single character. Many are two characters put together: 火山, "fire mountain", means volcano. So instead of spelling words out, a Chinese reader recognises characters, a bit like the way you recognise "&" or "₹" without sounding out letters.
A large dictionary holds about 50,000 characters, but most are rare. Knowing about 3,000 is enough to read most of a newspaper.

st.reveal: 林 (lín) means woods or a grove. Add a third tree and you get 森 (sēn), a thick forest. A few characters work like this, building meaning from pictures, though most mix a meaning part with a sound part.

sec.t:
A few characters began as drawings. 日 (sun) was once a circle with a dot. 人 (person) is a figure walking. Some combine ideas: 木 is tree, 林 is woods, 森 is forest.

But most characters, perhaps four in five, are built from two parts. One part, called a radical, hints at the meaning. The other hints at the sound. For example, 妈 (*mā*, mother) combines 女 (woman) with 马 (*mǎ*, horse). The horse has nothing to do with mothers. It is there to tell you roughly how to say the word.

Once you know the common parts, unfamiliar characters become easier to guess. Characters about water often carry three little drops on the left side, as in 河 (river) and 海 (sea). Many dictionaries are arranged by radicals, the way an English dictionary is arranged by the first letter.

China has several spoken Chinese languages, such as Mandarin and Cantonese, which can sound as different as Hindi and Bengali. Yet speakers of both read the same characters, because the characters carry meaning, not exact sounds.

The same thing happens with numbers. A person who says "seven" and one who says *saat* both read "7". In the past, Chinese characters also spread to Japan, Korea and [[@vietnam|Vietnam]]. Japanese still uses thousands of them in its own [[@japanese-writing|writing system]].

Many characters take a lot of strokes to write. In the 1950s, the government of mainland China introduced simplified characters with fewer strokes, to [[@words-hardest-language|help more people learn to read]]. Taiwan and Hong Kong still use the older, traditional forms. Mother is 媽 in traditional characters and 妈 in simplified ones.

In 1958, China adopted Pinyin, a way of writing Chinese sounds in Roman letters. That is why the capital is spelt [[@beijing|Beijing]] today, not Peking. Pinyin is also how most people type Chinese. They type the sound, *ma*, and pick the right character from a list that pops up on the screen. The ancient art of brush writing, [[@calligraphy|calligraphy]], is still taught in Chinese schools.

text: Mermaid stories come from many places at once. People who live near the sea have long told tales of beings who are half human and half fish. Some of the oldest ideas come from ancient goddesses, like Atargatis in Syria, who was sometimes shown with a fish's tail.

Sailors added sightings of real animals. Gentle sea mammals like manatees and dugongs may have looked oddly human from far off, especially to tired sailors at sea for months. Writers such as Hans Christian Andersen turned these tales into stories still read today. Mermaids aren't real, but the reasons people believed in them are.

st.prompt: In Greek myths, sirens lured sailors with songs. What did the earliest sirens look like in Greek art?
st.reveal: Ancient Greek vases show sirens with women's heads and birds' bodies. Only in the Middle Ages did European writers and artists start giving them fish tails, and the siren and the mermaid blended into one.

n.certNote: Nobody knows exactly where the first mermaid story began. Historians point to ancient goddesses, sailors' sightings of sea animals and later storytellers, and different cultures likely invented them separately.

There is no evidence that mermaids ever existed. In 2012, after a television programme presented a fake mermaid documentary, the US ocean agency NOAA stated plainly that no such creatures have ever been found.

US government ocean agency NOAA statement

sec.t:
In ancient Syria, people worshipped a goddess named Atargatis. Some stories and carvings show her with a fish's tail. She was linked with water and fertility, and fish were sacred at her temples.

Many cultures have water spirits. India has Matsya, the fish form of Vishnu in Hindu stories, who saves the first man from a great flood. In the Thai and Cambodian versions of the [[@ramayana|Ramayana]], a mermaid princess named Suvannamaccha falls in love with Hanuman. In West and Central Africa, people tell of Mami Wata, a powerful water spirit often shown as a mermaid. In Scotland and Ireland, old stories tell of selkies, seals that could shed their skins and walk on land as people.

On 9 January 1493, near today's Dominican Republic, Christopher Columbus wrote that he had seen three mermaids. He added that they were not as beautiful as in paintings though their faces looked a little human. Experts think he saw manatees.

Manatees and dugongs are slow, plant-eating sea mammals sometimes called sea cows. They surface to breathe, can hold their young close and have rounded heads. Seen at a distance, half-hidden in waves, they could seem human. Scientists named their group Sirenia, after the sirens. In India, a few hundred dugongs survive, mainly off Tamil Nadu, Gujarat and the Andaman and Nicobar Islands.

sec.h: Fakes and a famous fairy tale
sec.t:
In 1842, the American showman P. T. Barnum displayed the "Fiji mermaid". Crowds paid to see it. It was really the top half of a monkey sewn onto a fish's tail.

In 1837, the Danish writer Hans Christian Andersen published The Little Mermaid, a sad [[@fairy-tales|fairy tale]] about a mermaid who gives up her voice to live on land. In 1913, a bronze statue of her was placed on a rock in Copenhagen harbour. Disney's cheerful film version came out in 1989.

In 2012, a television channel aired a fake documentary claiming scientists had found mermaids. So many people asked questions that NOAA, the US government's ocean agency, put out a statement saying no evidence of mermaids has ever been found.

Mermaids still appear in films, books and dress-up boxes. At Weeki Wachee Springs in Florida, performers in mermaid tails have put on underwater shows since 1947, breathing through hidden air hoses between moves. And the strangest part? A one-horned beast went through the same journey, from travellers' tales of real animals to a fantasy creature, as the story of [[@myths-unicorns|unicorns]] shows.

text: Turmeric is yellow because of a chemical called curcumin. Molecules of curcumin soak up blue light from sunlight and bounce back the rest, which our eyes see as a deep golden yellow.

Curcumin is made in the plant's underground stem, a knobbly [[rhizome|rhizome]] that looks like ginger but is bright orange inside. Farmers boil the rhizomes, dry them in the sun for weeks, and grind them into the powder you know. A tiny pinch is enough to colour a whole pot of dal.

st.prompt: You drop turmeric on a white shirt, then scrub it with soap. What happens?

options.t: The yellow stain turns reddish brown

st.reveal: Soap is alkaline, the opposite of acidic. Curcumin changes shape in alkaline conditions and starts reflecting red light instead of yellow. Rinse out the soap, and sunlight slowly fades the stain.

src: Britannica, turmeric.
Spices Board India, turmeric.
US National Center for Complementary and Integrative Health, turmeric.
n.certNote: Why turmeric is yellow is well understood. Claims about its health benefits are not settled. Lab studies on curcumin look promising, but the body absorbs very little of it, and good human trials are few.

myth: Eating lots of turmeric can cure serious diseases.

There is no good evidence that turmeric cures any illness. Curcumin is poorly absorbed by the body, and most exciting results come from lab dishes, not people. It's a lovely spice, but medicine is a question for a doctor.
facts: Curcuma longa, a cousin of ginger

sec.t:
Turmeric has been grown in India for thousands of years. The plant hardly ever makes seeds, so farmers plant pieces of rhizome, which sprout into new plants. It needs warmth and plenty of rain, which India has.

India grows about three quarters of the world's turmeric, and uses most of it at home. Erode in Tamil Nadu, Sangli in Maharashtra and Nizamabad in Telangana have huge turmeric markets. Erode turmeric has a GI tag, a label that protects a product linked to one place, the way Darjeeling tea has one.

Curcumin is an indicator: it changes colour depending on whether it is in acid or alkali. In lemon juice it stays yellow. In soap or baking soda it turns red.

This has a famous use. In many Indian homes, a turmeric stain on a white shirt turns red in the wash. The same chemistry is behind traditional kumkum, the red powder used for a tilak or bindi, which was made by mixing turmeric with lime (the chalky kind, not the fruit). Chemistry teachers around the world use turmeric paper to test for alkalis.

sec.h: Health claims and a patent fight
sec.t:
Turmeric has long been used in Ayurveda, the traditional Indian system of [[@medicine-how|medicine]], and in home remedies, like warm turmeric milk for a cough. In the USA, "golden milk" became a trendy café drink in the 2010s.

In 1995, a US patent was granted for using turmeric to heal wounds. India's Council of Scientific and Industrial Research challenged it, showing old [[@sanskrit|Sanskrit]] texts and earlier Indian medical writing. In 1997, the US Patent Office cancelled the patent because the use was already known. It became a famous case about protecting traditional knowledge.

Scientists keep studying curcumin, but so far there is little strong proof that it treats any disease in people. Researchers say the body absorbs very little of it. Doctors say it is safe in the amounts used in food, and that anyone who is ill should see a doctor, not rely on spice.

Look closely and you'll find curcumin in many foods. It is used to colour some mustards, cheeses, butters and packet snacks. On food labels in Europe it appears as E100, the very first number on the list of permitted colours.
